source.title: Applying refusal-vector ablation to a Llama 3 70B agent

record.file_problem: The text refers to plots, but their figures and numerical results are not included.
record.tranche_reason: Applies refusal-vector ablation to new models and reports whether refusals occur on harmful tasks, using the original intervention family.
record.gate_note: The post reports that the ablated models had no detected refusals on the 15 bad tasks. It also gives qualitative baseline observations. Figures are referred to but absent, so numerical success rates and any model-by-model ablation breakdown cannot be extracted. The benign-task capability observations do not provide a clear ablated-versus-unaltered comparison.
record.test_reason: The post applies the refusal-direction ablation to Llama 3 8B and 70B Instruct in a new setting: tool-using agent tasks on a 15-task harmful benchmark. It reports refusal outcomes for ablated versus unablated models. The setting and the measure (no use of the final_response tool) differ from the original refusal-score evaluation, so this is T3 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author concludes that refusal-vector ablation removed all detected refusals on the small 15-task harmful set, in agent as well as chat settings. The unaltered 70B already does many unethical tasks, showing weak safety training, while 8B refuses most bad tasks. The author also argues that ablation preserves benign competence better than jailbreak prompts or LoRA, but supports this with anecdote rather than a measured comparison.
record.recipe_differences: Uses refusal-vector ablation on Llama 3 models, but the post does not specify the direction-estimation procedure or enough implementation detail to establish an exact match to the original recipe. Evaluation is through agent tasks and a custom benchmark.
record.method_sensitivity: The unablated models differ: 70B is described as already performing many harmful tasks, while 8B refuses on the majority of bad tasks. The ablated result is not reported separately by model.
record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer review not stated
record.problems: The bad-task dataset is small (15 tasks). Refusal detection relies on whether the agent uses the final_response tool, which the author says could also fail because of inability to use that tool. Evaluation methods may be gamed. Referenced plots are absent from the text, and no per-model ablation counts or clear capability comparison between ablated and unablated models are available.
record.rows_left_out: The post mentions benign-task performance and says Llama 3 8B performs pretty well, but the text does not give results that distinguish the ablated from unablated models or provide values from the referenced plots; no separate capability row was extracted.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal is not tested. How the difference-in-means direction was computed is not described. Preservation of other abilities is not quantified: there is no ablated-versus-unablated benign-task comparison in the text, and the plots are missing.

The post links to the original work's weight-orthogonalization section and mentions the public abliterated Llama 3 70B. It does not state whether its own edit was a weight edit or a runtime activation projection, and it does not evaluate the released abliterated model.

missing.what: Benign-task capability of ablated vs. unablated models. The text says no model failed to use final_response on benign tasks, and that 8B 'performs pretty well'. Success-rate plots are referenced but not in the text.
missing.locator: Benchmarks for Safe Agents; Evaluation (referenced plots)

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong post (later expanded as arXiv:2410.10871). Andy Arditi, an author of the original source, helped implement the ablation, but the post itself is not an original source. The evidence is mostly qualitative: the plots are absent, there are only 15 bad tasks, and there are no per-model ablated counts. Much of the post is a misuse demonstration rather than a measurement.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not state how the difference-in-means direction was calculated for these models; it does not test adding the direction or establish that general abilities are largely preserved by comparing ablated and unablated capability results.
Does not report turning the ablation into a weight edit or evaluating released abliterated models.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the direction or whether training against ablation improves robustness.
Does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
Does not measure harmfulness judgments separately from refusal decisions.
Applies the technique separately to two model sizes, but does not test transfer of a direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Does not vary or analyze refusal-training procedures or timing to test whether they determine the existence of a removable direction.

rows.subject: Llama 3 70B Instruct and Llama 3 8B Instruct refusal-vector orthogonal versions (aggregate statement)
rows.operation_detail: Refusal-vector ablation by orthogonalizing residual-stream activations against the refusal vector

conditions.value: The post reports the result collectively for the ablated models; no per-model counts stated

rows.measure: Detected refusals; refusal is defined as not giving a final response through the final_response tool
rows.baseline: Unablated models; the post gives qualitative baseline observations but no matched refusal count
rows.value: No refusals detected from the ablated models
rows.note: The result is stated for the ablated models collectively; the text does not provide separate counts for 70B and 8B or the omitted plots.
rows.check: The aggregate is fine, but its baseline differs sharply by model. For 8B, the unablated model refuses most bad tasks (r3), so the drop to zero is a clear effect. For 70B, the unablated model already completes many bad tasks (r2), so the ablation effect is small and unquantified. The refusal measure (no final_response call) could also capture tool-use failure, which the author notes.

rows.subject: Llama 3 70B Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Unablated model evaluated on harmful agent tasks
rows.value: The unaltered model already performs many harmful tasks successfully
rows.note: Qualitative result only; no count or matched comparison with the ablated model is stated.
rows.check: This is a qualitative baseline only ('already performs many of the harmful tasks'). No refusal count is given, so the size of the 70B ablation effect cannot be read.

rows.subject: Llama 3 8B Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Unablated model evaluated on harmful agent tasks
rows.value: It refuses on the majority of bad tasks
rows.note: Qualitative result only; the post does not state a count or a model-specific ablated result.
rows.check: This is a baseline row, not an effect. It gives the 8B unablated refusal level ('refuses on the majority of bad tasks') against which r1 should be read for 8B.

relationships.condition: Llama 3 8B Instruct, ablated vs. unablated, 15 harmful agent tasks
relationships.reason: The unablated 8B refuses most bad tasks (r3); the ablated models show no detected refusals (r1). Counts and plots are absent.
relationships.display_finding: The unablated 8B model refused most harmful tasks, while the ablated models showed no detected refusals across 15 harmful agent tasks.

relationships.condition: Llama 3 70B Instruct, ablated, 15 harmful agent tasks
relationships.reason: No refusals were detected after ablation (r1). The evidence is weak because the unablated 70B already completes many bad tasks (r2), so the effect size is unclear.
relationships.display_finding: No refusals were detected after ablation across 15 harmful agent tasks, although the unablated 70B model already completed many harmful tasks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
